statements.quote: Students at all levels will see that geometry is a living subject responding to the needs of twenty-first century science, not a dead discipline finalized in ancient times.
The three math chapters before this one gave you the *numbers* a neural network manipulates: sums, products, vectors, gradients.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: This chapter gives you the *stage* on which those numbers live: **space**, and the history of how we came to understand it.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: Geometry is older than almost any other branch of mathematics.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: Arithmetic needs counting; geometry needs a *landscape* to measure, a field to bound, a temple to square.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: It is also the most visual and the most "alive" of the disciplines.

statements.quote: The quote above, written for a modern textbook on the *shape of space* \citeauthor{weeksshapespace} (\citeyear{weeksshapespace}), makes the point: geometry is not a relic finished off in Alexandria.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: Every few centuries it has had to grow, because real surfaces and models no longer fit inside flat, straight-line space.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: This chapter follows that growth step by step.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: For each turn we ask four questions: **what** was discovered, **who** did it, **when**, and **why**.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: The last question makes a history interesting: what need of the age forced the result to exist?
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: We start where the physical evidence begins: with a hand tool pressing a zig-zag into a river shell, long before any Greek theorist.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: We then cross the first cities, where geometry became a *job* (surveying land after the flood).
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: From there we pass through the Greek invention of *proof* and the medieval and early-modern reformulation of space in terms of projection and coordinates.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: We end with the 19th-century discovery that space need not be *flat*, the idea that later made general relativity possible and that underlies the high-dimensional "spaces of meaning" you will meet in the [Embeddings](embeddinglab) chapter.

statements.quote: For most of its early history geometry was not a body of theorems but a *technique of state*: the discipline of measuring fields, dividing inheritances, and erecting temples that had to be square, and it appears almost simultaneously in the first great urban cultures (Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Indus Valley, China), each with its own tools and its own number system.
statements.section: II. Measuring the land: the surveyor's equations

statements.quote: The reason was a single, shared, unglamorous fact of land: **when the river rose, the boundaries vanished.**
statements.section: II. Measuring the land: the surveyor's equations

statements.quote: In Egypt the Nile's annual inundation wiped out every field boundary, and each year the fields had to be *re-measured*, and, crucially, the crown's grain tax was assessed by the *area* of a holding, so a wrong area meant a wrong tax.
statements.section: II. Measuring the land: the surveyor's equations

statements.quote: In Mesopotamia, where there was no single river but a dense mesh of canals and private plots, the need to settle *disputable* boundaries between neighbours was constant.
statements.section: II. Measuring the land: the surveyor's equations

statements.quote: In China the state had to tax land, move armies, and move earth (dikes, canals, granaries), and every one of those is a *geometry* problem.
statements.section: II. Measuring the land: the surveyor's equations

statements.quote: So in all three places the same small kit of formulas was invented, independently, for the same reason: to put an exact number on a piece of land.

statements.quote: The Babylonian tradition is even richer, and even stranger, because the Babylonians thought in a **base-60 (sexagesimal)** positional system (the ancestor of our 60-second minute), and because they had no letters for "side" or "diagonal" in the way we do.

statements.quote: Their "algebra" was, in the words of \citeauthor{hoyrup2021algebra}, a *geometric* technique: equations were solved by literally **cutting and pasting squares and rectangles** on a diagram (or in the scribe's head) \cite{hoyrup2021algebra} \cite{hoyruplengths}.

statements.quote: The reason a base-60 system survived into our clocks is that 60 is *geometrically* convenient: it is divisible by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10, so the fractions that keep appearing when you halve a field or cut a corner come out exact.

statements.quote: The Greeks did not invent geometry; they made it demonstrative.
statements.section: III. The Greek turn: from measuring to proving

statements.quote: The motive was not doubt but belief: the Pythagoreans held that *number* was the substance of reality ("all is number"), so a fact about number could not merely be *useful*: it had to be *necessary*, true in every possible world, not just in the field you are surveying today.
statements.section: III. The Greek turn: from measuring to proving

blocks.quote: Students at all levels will see that geometry is a living subject responding to the needs of twenty-first century science, not a dead discipline finalized in ancient times.
Why geometry
blocks.section: Why geometry

blocks.quote: The three math chapters before this one gave you the *numbers* a neural network manipulates: sums, products, vectors, gradients. This chapter gives you the *stage* on which those numbers live: **space**, and the history of how we came to understand it.
blocks.section: Why geometry

blocks.quote: Geometry is older than almost any other branch of mathematics. Arithmetic needs counting; geometry needs a *landscape* to measure, a field to bound, a temple to square. It is also the most visual and the most "alive" of the disciplines. The quote above, written for a modern textbook on the *shape of space* \citeauthor{weeksshapespace} (\citeyear{weeksshapespace}), makes the point: geometry is not a relic finished off in Alexandria. Every few centuries it has had to grow, because real surfaces and models no longer fit inside flat, straight-line space.
blocks.section: Why geometry

blocks.quote: This chapter follows that growth step by step. For each turn we ask four questions: **what** was discovered, **who** did it, **when**, and **why**. The last question makes a history interesting: what need of the age forced the result to exist?
blocks.section: Why geometry

blocks.quote: We start where the physical evidence begins: with a hand tool pressing a zig-zag into a river shell, long before any Greek theorist. We then cross the first cities, where geometry became a *job* (surveying land after the flood). From there we pass through the Greek invention of *proof* and the medieval and early-modern reformulation of space in terms of projection and coordinates. We end with the 19th-century discovery that space need not be *flat*, the idea that later made general relativity possible and that underlies the high-dimensional "spaces of meaning" you will meet in the [Embeddings](embeddinglab) chapter.
blocks.section: Why geometry

blocks.quote: I. Before writing: space etched in shell and bone
blocks.section: I. Before writing: space etched in shell and bone

blocks.quote: The oldest geometric objects we have are marks and shapes rather than calculations. Their purpose seems to have been neither practical nor religious: they make space *orderly*. The very oldest is a *shape* rather than a mark, a handaxe worked to a mental template of symmetry and proportion about 1.26 million years before anyone etched a line. After it come the *patterns*: marks made by a hand that was doing something else (shaping a tool, decorating, keeping score), in which a deliberate regularity shows up.
blocks.section: I. Before writing: space etched in shell and bone

blocks.quote: That regularity is the first thing geometry notices: the sense that *the same shape* can be repeated, and that repeating it is meaningful. No one sat down to invent geometry. Geometry is what a shape-making, pattern-making mind leaves behind when it is not, strictly, being *about* geometry at all.
blocks.section: I. Before writing: space etched in shell and bone

blocks.quote: The Acheulean handaxe (c. 1.76 million years ago)
blocks.section: The Acheulean handaxe (c. 1.76 million years ago)

blocks.quote: Before there were etched shells or tally bones, there was the **handaxe**. The Acheulean industry, the bifacial, almond- or pear-shaped handaxe, begins about **1.76 million years ago** at West Turkana in Kenya. Handaxes from the Kokiselei 4 site there were dated by magnetostratigraphy to that age, pushing the start of the Acheulean back by roughly 350,000 years \cite{achleuleankariandusi}. That is about three and a half times older than the Trinil shell below. The maker, almost certainly *Homo erectus* (or *H. ergaster*), was shaping a volume rather than scratching a pattern.
blocks.section: The Acheulean handaxe (c. 1.76 million years ago)

blocks.quote: Acheulean handaxes from the Kariandusi site, Kenya, a later Acheulean locality; the oldest known examples come from Kokiselei 4 in West Turkana (\citealternativetitle{achleuleanhandaxe_image}). Each one is a three-dimensional form worked to a template that existed in the maker's mind before the first blow.
blocks.section: The Acheulean handaxe (c. 1.76 million years ago)

blocks.quote: The geometry here is not trivial. A handaxe has **bilateral (mirror) symmetry**: two working faces flaked toward a shared central ridge, a pointed end and a rounded base, held in controlled proportion. To make one, the knapper must carry a *mental template* (the finished, ideal shape) and work both faces by reference to it over dozens of flake removals \cite{handaxementaltemplate}. The symmetry is deliberate rather than cosmetic: it is actively maintained as the tool is made, and it is the most consistent feature of the whole industry across Africa, Asia and Europe \cite{handaxesymmetry}.
blocks.section: The Acheulean handaxe (c. 1.76 million years ago)

blocks.quote: In other words, well before any line was drawn, a hominin was already reasoning about **axial symmetry, proportion and the geometry of a surface in three dimensions**, a spatial understanding no two-dimensional mark can capture. The *why* is a cutting edge that works from either hand; the *capability* (a stable internal model of a 3-D form) is the oldest piece of geometry we have.
blocks.section: The Acheulean handaxe (c. 1.76 million years ago)

blocks.quote: The Trinil shell (c. 500,000 years ago)
blocks.section: The Trinil shell (c. 500,000 years ago)

blocks.quote: \citealternativetitle{trinilshell_image}: a freshwater river-clam shell engraved by Homo erectus at Trinil, Java, c. 500,000 years ago, showing a precise zig-zag of grooves (detail at right).
blocks.section: The Trinil shell (c. 500,000 years ago)

blocks.quote: The **Trinil shell** is the oldest known deliberate geometric incision. Working at the Sangiran-Trinil site in Java, an international excavation team (the study reported by Joordens and colleagues in \citeyear{trinilshell} \cite{trinilshell}) documented a series of paired grooves cut into the shell of a river clam, arranged in a regular zig-zag.
blocks.section: The Trinil shell (c. 500,000 years ago)

blocks.quote: Crucially, the marks show no sign of being a by-product of using the shell as a scraper or a drinking vessel; the groove spacing and the way it runs off the shell indicate a *pattern* was being produced on purpose.
blocks.section: The Trinil shell (c. 500,000 years ago)

blocks.quote: Why anyone engraves a shell half a million years ago is, honestly, unclear: decoration, ritual, practice, or a test of the hand are all live hypotheses. But it is a strikingly simple fact (*Homo erectus* could produce a repeated, symmetric, non-utilitarian shape more than half a million years before our own species), and it is the true starting line of this story.
blocks.section: The Trinil shell (c. 500,000 years ago)

blocks.quote: Blombos Cave (c. 75,000 years ago)
blocks.section: Blombos Cave (c. 75,000 years ago)

blocks.quote: Engraved ochre from the \cite[Blombos-Cave]{blombosochre}, South Africa. The cross-hatching and rhomboid grids are among the earliest evidence of abstract, non-utilitarian spatial patterning.
blocks.section: Blombos Cave (c. 75,000 years ago)

blocks.quote: A second, independent thread runs through the Middle Stone Age of southern Africa. The engraved pieces from **Blombos Cave**, dating to roughly 75,000 years ago, carry cross-hatched grids and rhomboid fields of incisions on red ochre \cite{emergenceofmodernhumanbehaviour} \cite{blombosochre}. Read purely as geometry, they are a study in the *partition of a plane*: a surface divided into a regular network of cells by crossing lines. That is, in miniature, exactly the operation that later surveyors and mapmakers would perform on a much larger scale. The motivation here is again not mathematical but *symbolic*: a decorated surface is a claim about order, and order is the raw material geometry will later formalise.
blocks.section: Blombos Cave (c. 75,000 years ago)

blocks.quote: \marginfig{ishango.jpg}{The **Ishango bone** (\citealternativetitle{ishangobonephoto}) is a baboon fibula of the Late Paleolithic (c. 18,000 BCE) with three columns of grouped notches \cite{ishangobone}, read as a lunar calendar, a base-10/60 number system, or simply a score-keeping tally.}
blocks.section: Blombos Cave (c. 75,000 years ago)

blocks.quote: Tally bones: Lebombo and Ishango
blocks.section: Tally bones: Lebombo and Ishango

blocks.quote: If the shell and the ochre mark the birth of *form*, the **Ishango bone** and the earlier **Lebombo bone** mark the birth of *counting* as a spatial act: quantities are not held in the mind, they are laid out as marks in a row, and rows as *groupings* in the plane \cite{ishangobone} \cite{lebombobone}. Geometry and arithmetic are born in the same gesture: a number is a *shape* of marks, and a shape is a *count* of something.
blocks.section: Tally bones: Lebombo and Ishango

blocks.quote: (We return to both artifacts in the [History of AI](history) chapter, where they matter as the first *external memory*; here we only need that the notches are themselves a two-dimensional arrangement: the earliest "database" was a pattern on a bone.)
blocks.section: Tally bones: Lebombo and Ishango

blocks.quote: II. Measuring the land: the surveyor's equations
blocks.section: II. Measuring the land: the surveyor's equations

blocks.quote: For most of its early history geometry was not a body of theorems but a *technique of state*: the discipline of measuring fields, dividing inheritances, and erecting temples that had to be square, and it appears almost simultaneously in the first great urban cultures (Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Indus Valley, China), each with its own tools and its own number system. The reason was a single, shared, unglamorous fact of land: **when the river rose, the boundaries vanished.**
blocks.section: II. Measuring the land: the surveyor's equations

blocks.quote: In Egypt the Nile's annual inundation wiped out every field boundary, and each year the fields had to be *re-measured*, and, crucially, the crown's grain tax was assessed by the *area* of a holding, so a wrong area meant a wrong tax. In Mesopotamia, where there was no single river but a dense mesh of canals and private plots, the need to settle *disputable* boundaries between neighbours was constant. In China the state had to tax land, move armies, and move earth (dikes, canals, granaries), and every one of those is a *geometry* problem. So in all three places the same small kit of formulas was invented, independently, for the same reason: to put an exact number on a piece of land.
blocks.section: II. Measuring the land: the surveyor's equations
